opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few reasons, and they're mostly historical and practical rather than some deep principled reason.

Part of it is just that pre-training was the thing that worked first. We had a really clean recipe: you take the internet, you predict the next token, you scale up compute, and the loss goes down very predictably. That predictability is enormously valuable when you're deciding where to put hundreds of millions of dollars. You can draw the scaling curve and be fairly confident about what you'll get. RL has historically been much less like that. It's finicky, it's unstable, and you'd often spend a lot of compute and get very little out, or the model would find some weird reward hack and you'd have to start over.

The second piece is that RL on language models really only started working in a robust way fairly recently. For a long time, post-training was mostly about shaping behavior. RLHF was about making the model helpful and nice to talk to, not about teaching it fundamentally new capabilities. You don't need that much compute to do that. It's more like steering than building.

What's changed is that once you have a strong enough base model, RL on verifiable rewards, things like math, competitive programming, and eventually real software engineering tasks, actually starts teaching the model new skills. The model is good enough to sometimes get the right answer, so there's signal to reinforce. Before that point you just don't get any gradient that matters; the model never succeeds, so there's nothing to learn from.

And then there's an infrastructure lag. Pre-training infrastructure has been optimized for years. RL infrastructure is much messier: you need environments, you need sandboxes, you need to run inference at scale and feed that back into training, and you need good, unhackable reward signals. Building all of that takes time. So I think the gap in spend is less a statement of where the returns are and more a reflection of where the tooling has been. My expectation is that you'll see RL compute climb pretty dramatically and eventually become comparable to, or even exceed, pre-training. The returns look very real once you can actually scale it.

r001.rationale: It says pre-training was predictable while RL was historically finicky and unreliable, but does not explain lower RL spending as labs waiting for greater algorithmic confidence before large runs.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts pre-training’s clean, predictable recipe with RL’s messy infrastructure and instability; it does not describe RL as more amenable to incremental iteration.

r003.rationale: It predicts RL compute will climb dramatically and eventually become comparable to or exceed pre-training, communicating that the current spending gap will close.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that until pretty recently, nobody had shown that RL on language models scaled in the way pre-training did. Pre-training had this beautiful, almost boring property: you put in ten times more compute, you get a predictable drop in loss, and that loss translates into capabilities you care about. That's an incredibly easy thing to justify to whoever is signing off on a multi-billion dollar cluster. RL didn't have that story. Early RLHF was mostly about shaping behavior, making the model polite and helpful, and you could do that with a tiny fraction of the pre-training budget. It wasn't obvious that pouring more compute into it would give you a smarter model rather than just a more sycophantic one.

The second thing is that RL is just much harder to do well. With pre-training, the data is sitting there, the objective is fixed, and most of the engineering is about scaling the matrix multiplies. With RL, you need environments, you need reward signals that are actually correct and hard to game, and you need infrastructure that can do inference and training at the same time, which is a genuinely painful systems problem. If your reward model is slightly off, you spend all that compute teaching the model to exploit the flaw. So the compute was gated by how fast people could build verifiable tasks and robust reward pipelines, not by how many chips were available.

And then there's a path dependence thing. The labs built their whole stack around pre-training, and the people who knew how to scale pre-training were the ones with influence over allocation. It takes a demonstration, something like the reasoning models, where you can see verifiable domains like math and code improving sharply with more RL compute, before the organization believes it's worth shifting the balance. I think that demonstration has now happened, and you're seeing the ratio change pretty quickly. The interesting question going forward isn't whether RL gets more compute, it's how far the verifiable-reward regime extends into messier domains before you hit the limit of what you can cleanly score.

r001.rationale: The response says labs lacked evidence that RL scaled with compute and needed a demonstration of improved results before believing it justified shifting more compute to RL.

r002.rationale: It contrasts RL’s engineering and reward challenges with pre-training, but does not say RL is more amenable to incremental iteration.

r003.rationale: It says the demonstration has happened and the ratio of compute spending is changing quickly, predicting that RL spending will rise relative to pre-training.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that we knew how to turn more pre-training compute into better models reliably. You have an enormous amount of text, a simple objective, and scaling laws that give you some confidence that a bigger run will be worthwhile. Reinforcement learning has historically been much less predictable.

The bottleneck isn’t just how much compute you’re willing to spend. It’s what environments you have and what signal you’re training against. If you’re optimizing a reward model trained on human preferences, you can’t necessarily keep optimizing it forever. Eventually you discover ways to get a high score that don’t correspond to being more useful. So spending ten times as much compute doesn’t automatically buy you a better model.

There’s also a capability prerequisite. The model needs to occasionally produce something good for reinforcement learning to reinforce it. Pre-training gets you into a regime where the model can explore useful solutions, rather than just fail in a million different ways.

I’d expect that balance to shift as we get better at building tasks where you can check whether the model succeeded. Code is an obvious example: you can run it. If you have a reliable reward signal, sufficiently difficult problems, and a model that can make progress on them, then there’s a much stronger reason to spend substantial compute on reinforcement learning.

r001.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning has been less predictable than pre-training, but does not explain lower spending as labs waiting for more confidence in their algorithms before committing to large runs.

r002.rationale: It discusses RL’s dependence on environments and reward signals, but does not distinguish it as more amenable to incremental iteration than pre-training.

r003.rationale: It expects the balance to shift when better, checkable tasks become available, but does not predict that RL compute spending will stop trailing pre-training by much longer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to how reliably you can turn compute into better capabilities. With pre-training, you’ve got an enormous amount of text, a fairly simple objective, and a recipe where you can be reasonably confident that making the model bigger and training it longer will improve it.

With reinforcement learning, you have to build the environment and the reward signal. How do you tell whether an answer is actually good? For something like math or code, you can often check it. For a complicated research task, that’s much harder. And if your reward signal is imperfect, spending more compute can just make the model better at exploiting that imperfection.

There’s also a distinction between using RL to make a model more pleasant to interact with and using it to teach the model substantially new capabilities. If you’re mostly doing the former, you may get most of the benefit with a relatively small amount of compute. To justify spending something comparable to a pre-training run, you need a setup where the model can keep learning as you scale it. Building those setups is a substantial research problem.

r001.rationale: The response says RL needs reliable rewards and scalable learning setups, but does not clearly say labs are waiting for greater algorithmic confidence before committing to large runs.

r002.rationale: It contrasts small-compute interaction tuning with capability training, but does not characterize RL as more amenable to incremental iteration than pre-training.

r003.rationale: It gives no prediction about whether RL compute spending will soon approach pre-training spending.
